authors.name: Ernest Hemingway
authors.intro: A daughter waits outside her father’s apartment, holding his spare key. Stop the scene there, while you still know why she has come. Next morning, read the approach again. Has the key been in her hand long enough to grow warm? Has she rehearsed a greeting she cannot use? A correction can put you back outside that door, ready to open it. This is one use for Hemingway’s daily rereading. If the daughter is still on the doorstep a week later, rereading may be delaying the next scene.

authors.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
authors.intro: A generous landlord replaces a tenant’s broken stove. Then he photographs the receipt beside her eviction notice. The label has lasted one sentence. You now have to decide what his generosity buys him, and whether he knows it. Fitzgerald’s selected advice directs attention to particular people and the verbs that reveal them. An outline can arrange this encounter; it cannot settle the landlord’s character in advance. If he enters only to prove that landlords are generous, or that they are cruel, the stove has become an expensive illustration of something you already decided.

authors.name: Stephen King
authors.intro: “I’m pleased for you,” she said bitterly. Remove bitterly and the remark could be sincere. Put it after the speaker tears up an invitation, and the adverb may repeat what we have seen. Put it in an otherwise cordial conversation, and cutting it can erase the grievance. King’s advice makes a useful demand on the surrounding scene: can the speech and action carry the tone? Deleting the modifier is easy. The harder revision gives us a reason to hear the bitterness without being told it is there.

authors.name: Ray Bradbury
authors.intro: A man waits outside a locked café. If the owner arrives, we may have a story about an appointment. If the man stays after learning that the owner is dead, the waiting means something else. A short story lets you reach that difference before you have spent a year on the opening. Bradbury’s weekly-story challenge encourages this kind of finished attempt. His emphasis on enjoyment needs more care. A difficult second page does not prove that the first was a mistake. Try another ending before deciding you have chosen the wrong story.

authors.name: William Zinsser
authors.intro: “Service interruptions may be experienced” leaves a tenant wondering what to plan for. “The water will be off from noon to two” gives an answer. But the same briskness may damage a family memory. An aunt who takes three paragraphs to admit that she misses her sister may be telling us something through the delay. Zinsser distinguishes the demands of different kinds of nonfiction. A notice needs to get the water shutoff across. A memoir may need us to hear the person who cannot get to the point. Revise for the reader’s particular need before making every sentence shorter.

authors.name: Kurt Vonnegut
authors.intro: A woman must cross town before the pharmacy closes. Her bus passes without stopping. Now the timetable matters, and the next action will tell us something about her. Does she run, call someone, or turn back? Vonnegut’s advice puts desire under pressure; it does not require a catastrophe. The missed bus is enough if we know what the woman needs. Telling us her destination has not given the story away. We still do not know what she will sacrifice to reach it, or what she will do if she cannot.

authors.name: Toni Morrison
authors.angle: How much of the book one character gets
authors.intro: The sister who ruins dinner has eleven minutes before her shift. The host wants to eat; the sister needs to ask for money before she goes to work. Giving her that urgency does not excuse her behavior. It gives her something to do besides inconvenience the protagonist. Morrison later regretted an underwritten character while describing the need to restrain another who threatened to dominate a book. Both problems appear in this small scene. The sister needs a purpose of her own, and the writer still has to decide whether her eleven minutes deserve two lines or a chapter.

authors.name: Edgar Allan Poe
authors.intro: A passenger learns that her train will not stop at the town printed on her ticket. To make the scene frightening, let the conductor recognize the town and refuse to discuss it. To make it comic, let every passenger produce the same obsolete ticket. The route is unchanged; the details tell us how to receive the journey. Poe’s account of composition makes the intended effect govern such choices. Try deciding the effect before writing the next exchange. Then notice what you have to suppress to keep it: a laugh, an awkward fact, a passenger who refuses to be frightened.

authors.name: Margaret Atwood
authors.intro: “The guests arrived late.” The host watches the food cool. A visitor is still looking for the address. A child hopes nobody will arrive at all. Late is already somebody’s judgment. In her 1990 interview, Atwood questions the assumption that a powerful country’s experience stands for everyone’s. A narrator can make a smaller version of that mistake, treating one person’s expectations as the natural arrangement of the world. Give the host a confident sentence. Then imagine the guest who would find it peculiar. You may discover a quarrel before anybody reaches the table.

authors.name: David Ogilvy
authors.angle: What a memo asks its reader to do
authors.intro: The memo is only three sentences long. Nobody can act on it: “The room is unavailable. Several alternatives were discussed. A decision is needed.” Who must decide? By when? Replace it with “Please choose the library or the studio by noon so I can confirm the booking.” The recipient now has a job. Ogilvy wrote his instructions for colleagues whose prose had to produce decisions. The two-page limit makes sense in that setting. Even a short memo can leave its actual request for the recipient to write.

items.title: Study a manual
items.text: Return repeatedly to Roman and Raphaelson’s Writing That Works.

items.title: Conversational language
items.text: Use a natural speaking manner when composing workplace prose.

items.title: Small units
items.text: Prefer compact words, sentences, and paragraphs for business writing.

items.title: Drop the costume
items.text: Avoid inflated jargon that makes the writer seem self-important.

items.title: A page limit
items.text: Keep the correspondence covered by this memo within two pages.

items.title: Check the borrowing
items.text: Verify quotations before allowing them to carry your argument.

items.title: An overnight gap
items.text: Wait until morning, then read aloud and revise before sending.

items.title: A colleague’s help
items.text: Invite a colleague to improve an especially consequential message.

items.title: State the request
items.text: Make clear what you want the recipient to do.

items.title: Choose the channel
items.text: Consider a direct conversation when action is the immediate goal.

authors.name: John Steinbeck
authors.intro: The toothbrush is yellow. Or should it be blue? You can spend an afternoon on this question without deciding who left it in the bathroom. Let someone arrive: a brother with nowhere to sleep, an unfamiliar guest, the woman who lives there and has forgotten buying a spare. Each arrival changes the object. Choosing the color has not yet told you who brought it. Steinbeck’s advice is useful when small corrections keep delaying the rest of a draft. The color may matter later, once someone has entered the room.

items.title: Shrink today’s assignment
items.text: Attend to the day’s page rather than the enormous unfinished whole.
items.context: February 1962 letter to Robert Wallsten.

items.title: Draft beyond the corrections
items.text: Get the whole draft down before revision interrupts its momentum.
items.context: February 1962 letter to Robert Wallsten.

items.title: Address one reader
items.text: Imagine a particular reader instead of an intimidating anonymous audience.
items.context: February 1962 letter to Robert Wallsten.

items.title: Leave a gap
items.text: Pass a resistant scene; the completed draft may reveal its purpose.
items.context: February 1962 letter to Robert Wallsten.

items.title: Distrust the favorite scene
items.text: Check whether a cherished passage distorts the surrounding work.
items.context: February 1962 letter to Robert Wallsten.

items.title: Put speech in the mouth
items.text: Speak dialogue while composing it to hear whether it sounds spoken.
items.context: February 1962 letter to Robert Wallsten.

authors.name: Billy Wilder
authors.intro: A woman says she has stopped waiting for her brother. Later, she sets two plates, notices the second, and puts it away. The action contradicts her statement. But we must know whose plate it is; otherwise she could simply be laying too much cutlery. Wilder’s 1996 interview recalls Lubitsch solving a character problem through a hat. The inference depends on preparation. We need a reason to connect the extra place with her brother. After that, an explanation of how much she misses him may merely repeat what the plate has already told us.

items.title: Uncertain spectators
items.text: Expect an audience’s response to be difficult to predict.

items.title: Sustain the pressure
items.text: Secure attention early and maintain it throughout the film.

items.title: A legible pursuit
items.text: Give the protagonist an action the audience can follow.

items.title: Know the destination
items.text: Understand where the story is headed as you construct it.

items.title: Conceal the machinery
items.text: Keep necessary plot turns from drawing attention to the story’s structure.

items.title: Look upstream
items.text: An ending’s weakness may originate in the story’s opening.

items.title: Room for inference
items.text: Let spectators complete an implication instead of spelling it out.
items.context: Wilder credits this principle to Ernst Lubitsch.

items.title: Useful voice-over
items.text: Add information in narration instead of repeating visible action.

items.title: The decisive turn
items.text: Make the second act’s closing event initiate the final movement.

items.title: Finish at the finish
items.text: Accelerate the last act, then stop after the culminating event.

arguments.title: When to revise
arguments.dek: When correcting a sentence helps the next scene, and when it delays it.

blocks.text: A correction can improve the first paragraph while leaving the next scene unwritten.

Hemingway describes [[hemingway-4|rereading and correcting before continuing]]. Steinbeck’s [[steinbeck-2|letter to Robert Wallsten]] warns that revision can become an excuse for stopping. Both revise their work.

blocks.label: A draft
blocks.text: Mara put the key on the table. It was a strange thing to do. She had waited a long time for this.

“Strange” and “a long time” leave the important decisions unwritten. Why has Mara brought the key? Perhaps she is returning it because she will never enter the house again. Change put to slid and have her slide it toward her brother. Now the sentence asks for his response. The correction has given you a reason to go on.
Let him refuse it

Suppose you already know that he refuses the key. Another hour spent on put will not write that refusal. Let him push it back, cover it with his glass, or leave the room. Each action changes the meaning of the sentence you have been polishing. Only after the brother acts will you know whether slid is the right verb.

Hemingway’s rereading can restore the scene’s pace and the distance between its people. Steinbeck names the danger of doing it indefinitely. You can recognize that danger without adopting a permanent ban on revision: ask whether the last correction made another sentence possible.
One pass, then six sentences

Make one correction that affects what happens next. Then write six new sentences without returning to the opening. Read it again afterward. If the new scene has made the first sentence unnecessary, you have learned something that polishing could not tell you. If the opening contains a contradiction that makes the next action impossible, fix it now. Leaving a bad adjective is one thing; building a scene on an impossible action is another.

arguments.title: Must you know how it ends?
arguments.dek: The locksmith may be receiving threats. He may be receiving homework.

blocks.text: [[poe-1|Poe asks for the ending first]]. [[king-15|King favors discovery while writing]]. Try both approaches on the same locksmith.

blocks.label: One invented premise, two endings
blocks.text: Every Tuesday, a retired locksmith receives an envelope containing a key.
blocks.after:
Ending A: the keys open his own former homes.
Ending B: none opens anything; he has been teaching his grandson how to make them.

blocks.text: Ending A makes the envelopes a puzzle about memory or intrusion. Earlier scenes can plant addresses, altered locks, or the locksmith’s reluctance to visit one house. Ending B changes the envelopes into exercises and the locksmith into an anxious teacher. The same key can measure either a threat or an apprenticeship. Knowing the ending changes what counts as a useful detail.
The grandson sends a bent wire

Now let the grandson send a bent wire. Is it a joke, a refusal, or a tool the locksmith does not recognize? Both outlines have acquired a new problem. If the gesture is more interesting than the planned reveal, follow it for a scene before defending the ending.

Try two provisional endings before drafting the middle. For each, list three earlier details it would require. Then draft a scene that could make one ending impossible. If nothing can threaten your plan, the plan may be doing too much of the character’s thinking. If every new detail destroys the plan, decide what promise still holds the work together.
The finished poem and its explanation

Poe explains a finished poem; we cannot independently reconstruct its composition from that account. The locksmith exercise asks a separate question: what does choosing an ending now allow you to prepare, and what does it make you refuse? Treat the ending as a decision you can revise as the scene develops.

arguments.title: When the writing hour disappears
arguments.dek: Morrison’s early mornings began with childcare. Her hours changed as her life changed.

blocks.text: In the 1993 interview, [[morrison-1|Morrison describes writing before her children woke]]. Necessity became a preference. In the [[s:morrison-nea|later NEA interview]], her habits have changed with age.

Hemingway’s [[hemingway-2|stopping point]] offers another kind of preparation: leave yourself knowing what happens next. You can carry that instruction into a twenty-minute session, a borrowed room, or an evening interrupted by other work. The next action may be easier to preserve than the hour itself.

blocks.label: An original schedule experiment
blocks.text:
Tuesday: 25 minutes. Write the brother’s refusal.
Wednesday: read Tuesday’s last paragraph; write the consequence.
If interrupted: leave a sentence naming the next action.

There is something to resume on Wednesday. If Wednesday becomes Thursday because a child is ill, the consequences of the brother’s refusal are still there to write. The task survives the missed appointment. A routine described only as “write every morning” gives you less help when morning is unavailable.
Who can close the door?

King’s [[king-13|instruction to remove interruptions]] assumes some control over the writing space. If the table will be needed at nine, agree on the twenty minutes before it. If there is no room to close, decide which interruption can wait. You are trying to secure enough time to write the exchange, not reproduce another writer’s household.

For three sessions, note what you attempted, how long you had, and where you stopped. Then use the record. If the first ten minutes always disappear into rereading, leave a clearer starting point. If you repeatedly stop just as the scene begins, try one longer session. Change the arrangement that is failing instead of adding another rule to the day.

arguments.title: What does the reader need to know?
arguments.dek: A missing motive can sustain a scene. A missing address makes a bad invitation.

blocks.text: Steinbeck’s [[steinbeck-3|one imagined reader]] makes an anonymous audience less frightening. [[vonnegut-7|Vonnegut]] chooses a particular recipient too. But choosing someone to write to leaves another question: what must that person know? Ogilvy’s [[ogilvy-9|memo]] demands a clear next action. Wilder’s [[wilder-7|principle, credited to Lubitsch]], asks the audience to complete an implication. Consider what each instruction would do to this sentence.

blocks.label: The same original sentence in two places
blocks.text: The door will be open at seven.

In a story, this can be a promise, a warning, or an invitation the recipient dreads accepting. The uncertainty is usable if the scene gives us a reason to care. In an email to a contractor, the sentence may fail. Which door? Who will be there? Is the recipient expected to arrive at seven, or merely allowed to? A reader cannot carry out a request whose missing information has been mistaken for elegance.
The motive and the address

You can conceal why a character wants the visitor to arrive while stating exactly when and where they will meet. You can also explain the character’s feelings at length and still forget to name the street. Does the reader get to anticipate a confrontation, or do they have to ask for the address?

blocks.label: An original practical revision
blocks.text: Please meet the plumber at the side door of 18 King Street at 7 a.m. The key is under the blue pot.
The revision names the place, the person to meet, the time, and how to get in. Why the sender cannot attend may be irrelevant. In a story, that absence might be the thing we most want explained.

Write down one thing the reader must know now and one thing they may profitably discover later. Test those decisions on someone who has not seen the draft. Ask what they expect to happen, not whether they understood everything. A mistaken expectation may reveal a missing cue; an interesting expectation may be the pleasure you meant to create.

[[s:vonnegut-oc|Vonnegut names Flannery O’Connor as an exception]] to almost all his rules. Keep that admission beside the rules. A short story that withholds its situation may repay the reader later. A plumber left outside the wrong house is unlikely to admire the suspense.

arguments.title: Can you learn a voice without keeping it?
arguments.dek: Borrow a sentence’s rhythm. Check what it makes you invent.

blocks.text: The [[king-14|King list]] warns against imitation; his [[s:king-npr|memoir excerpt]] describes it as part of learning. [[s:zinsser-revisions|Zinsser writes about studying models]] and changing them. A writer can learn the cadence of a sentence before knowing when to resist it. Here is a small reason to resist.

blocks.label: An original sentence, three ways
blocks.text: The committee did not answer my letter.
blocks.after:
They filed it, discussed it, and forgot it.
For six weeks, the letter acquired everything except an answer.

blocks.text: The first revision gives the committee a sequence of actions. The second gives the delay a joke. But we know only that no answer arrived. Filed, discussed, and forgot may be three inventions added to make the sentence sound finished. Before keeping its rhythm, find out what the verbs claim.
A verb, a pause, a short last word

Choose one decision you can hear in a model: a delayed verb, a long sentence ending on a short word, an explanation replaced by an action. Use it on different material, then write a version without it. What did the borrowed arrangement make you add? What did it make you leave out?

Fitzgerald’s [[fitzgerald-6|letter about verbs]] makes this a concrete place to look. In our example, filed, discussed, and forgot give the institution three actions. They are more vivid than a description of bureaucratic indifference. They also require more knowledge of what happened to the letter.
If they never received the letter

Now imagine the committee never received the letter. The lively verbs have manufactured a story. Elegance cannot repair an unsupported fact. For nonfiction, check the action before strengthening it. A less vivid sentence can be the more exact one. For fiction, decide whether the narrator knows, guesses, or invents what the committee did; the difference can become part of the character.

Revise the paragraph once for rhythm and once for accuracy. Then combine what survives. If the joke still works, keep it. If it needs the committee to have done something you cannot know, decide whether the narrator is making an accusation, guessing, or reporting. Those are three different sentences, however similar they sound.

arguments.title: Who gets to take over the story?
arguments.dek: The sister has eleven minutes. The host thinks she has ruined dinner.

blocks.text: Morrison asks a writer to [[morrison-4|answer to characters]] and to [[morrison-5|control their share of the book]]. Her [[s:morrison-nea|later interview]] describes both an underwritten minor character and a dominant one who needed restraining. You can encounter both problems at the same dinner.

blocks.label: An original scene problem
blocks.text: The sister ruins dinner by asking to borrow money.

“Ruins” gives us the host’s verdict. The sister has a bill due in the morning and eleven minutes before her shift. Let her ask while the host is still serving. The interruption now carries two clocks: the meal the host has planned, and the deadline she cannot move.
Before you call her selfish

What happens when you call her “the selfish sister”? You can predict every gesture before she makes it. Open Culture extracts a proposition about persons and types from [[fitzgerald-4|the narrator of The Rich Boy]]. It is a narrator’s statement, not a personal instruction from Fitzgerald, but it gives this scene a test. Let the sister, working up the courage to ask for money, insist that the limping host sit down while she brings the plates. Her request will interrupt dinner; her attention to the host complicates the label.

[[s:atwood-pr|Atwood’s 1990 interview]] questions a powerful country’s assumption that its experience is universal. Our dinner scene makes a smaller comparison. The host takes for granted that everyone has an evening to spend at the table. The sister does not. Staying in the host’s viewpoint need not make the host’s assumption a fact.
Eleven minutes, two versions

Write the request once from the host’s position, watching the food cool, and once from the sister’s, watching the clock. Give each a detail the other fails to notice. Then return to the original viewpoint and keep just one change. A single viewpoint can still show what matters to both characters.
If the sister now makes every other character dull, reconsider her role. She may belong at the center, or her brief interruption may be enough. A shorter appearance can still show what she wants.

moments.title: An hour on two sentences
moments.setup: You have spent an hour on these two sentences. The brother still has not moved.
moments.example: Mara put the key on the table. Her brother did not take it.

choices.label: Read back once; change what releases the next action.
choices.reason: The key is waiting for a response. One pass backward might expose the detail that makes the brother move.
choices.counter: The scene has already supplied its next problem: the refusal. Another polish could postpone the encounter you came to write.
choices.experiment: Change one detail in the opening. Then write six new sentences without returning to it. In a second version, leave the opening alone and write six sentences immediately.
choices.compare: Which version gives the brother something to do? Keep the action that changes the scene.
choices.exception: Resolve a factual or logical contradiction first if continuing would build the scene on it.

choices.label: Leave the opening alone and write the refusal.
choices.reason: There is enough on the page to continue. A refusal can produce new information that the opening cannot supply by itself.
choices.counter: If you have lost the scene’s pace or physical arrangement, moving forward may only multiply the confusion.
choices.experiment: Put brackets around the sentence you dislike. Write until someone changes position, possession, or intention. Then read the opening again.
choices.compare: Did the new action tell you what the first sentence needs? Change only what it now makes necessary.
choices.exception: A wrong speaker or impossible sequence is worth correcting now.

moments.title: You have a key. No door.
moments.setup: A locksmith keeps receiving keys in the mail. You like the premise, but the story has no destination.
moments.example: The seventh envelope contained a key made of soft lead.

choices.label: Choose an ending and plant what it will need.
choices.reason: The lead key can become a clue once you know what it eventually opens—or why it must never open anything.
choices.counter: The object may become interesting only when someone handles it. A plan chosen too soon can dismiss a better consequence discovered in the scene.
choices.experiment: Invent two incompatible endings. Give each three details it needs earlier. Draft the scene that would eliminate one ending.
choices.compare: Which ending changes the meaning of the lead key? Prefer a consequence to a surprise pasted on at the end.
choices.exception: If the character makes an interesting refusal, let that evidence threaten the outline.

choices.label: Let the locksmith act before deciding the ending.
choices.reason: The lead key gives the locksmith a problem. Put it in his hand and discover what he tries before choosing what the event must mean.
choices.counter: A series of interesting actions can still fail to arrive anywhere. Test whether the beginning makes a promise the eventual ending can answer.
choices.experiment: Write three things the locksmith tries with the key. Let the third change what he wants. Only then propose an ending and plant one earlier clue.
choices.compare: Does the ending grow from the changed desire, or merely close the file?
choices.exception: If you are solving an intricate puzzle, an early design may prevent impossible mechanics.

moments.title: Twenty minutes before someone needs the table.
moments.setup: An early shift has taken the quiet hour you used to keep. Tonight you have twenty minutes and an unfinished scene.
moments.example: At 8:40, the apartment is finally quiet. At 9:00, someone will need the table.

choices.label: Give the twenty minutes one small, definite task.
choices.reason: Twenty minutes may be enough to write one exchange.
choices.counter: A short session can disappear into rereading. Leave a note naming the next action before the table is needed.
choices.experiment: Write the one thing a character refuses to say. Stop two minutes before the table is needed and name the next action in a separate line.
choices.compare: At the next session, does that line save you the work of starting over?
choices.exception: If fatigue makes the work unusable, sleep is a practical choice.

choices.label: End with the next action still clear.
choices.reason: Use some of the interval to enter the scene, then stop before you have exhausted its next move. That gives the next session a starting point.
choices.counter: The best stopping point also has to fit the life around it. If the twenty minutes are all you have, a small completed task may matter more than a well-chosen stopping point.
choices.experiment: Write until you know the next action. Stop there and name that action in one plain line. At the next session, write it before revising the note.
choices.compare: Does the remaining action make returning easier?
choices.exception: If stopping repeatedly keeps you from finishing anything, choose one small task to complete instead.

moments.title: Is the missing information doing any work?
moments.setup: You want the reader to keep going. You have left the central instruction—or perhaps the central motive—unstated.
moments.example: The door will be open at seven.

choices.label: Make the intended action unmistakable.
choices.reason: For an invitation or a request, the reader needs enough information to act without sending three follow-up questions.
choices.counter: In a scene, the action can be clear while the character’s motive remains uncertain.
choices.experiment: Rewrite the sentence as a useful message to a plumber. Then use it as the opening of a scene in which someone is afraid to arrive.
choices.compare: List what each version must disclose. Are you hiding an address or a motive?
choices.exception: Do not manufacture ambiguity in a message that someone must act on.

choices.label: Leave something for the reader to infer.
choices.reason: An earlier detail can let the reader infer why the open door matters.
choices.counter: A request still needs enough information for someone to act. Keep the uncertainty in the scene, not in the invitation to the plumber.
choices.experiment: Add one earlier detail that makes the open door matter. Write the response without explaining the character’s feelings. Then add an explicit explanation and compare.
choices.compare: Can a reader tell why the open door matters from the action and the earlier detail?
choices.exception: If every reader invents an unrelated reason, the scene may need another cue.

moments.title: What did the committee actually do?
moments.setup: The three verbs sound brisk. Only the unanswered letter is certain.
moments.example: The committee filed my letter, discussed it, and forgot it.

choices.label: Keep the verbs; test what each one means.
choices.reason: The sequence gives the committee a small drama. It is worth testing whether those actions are known, inferred, or invented.
choices.counter: Here, “forgot” may mean that no answer arrived, rather than that the letter left anyone’s memory. The vivid verb could name the wrong event.
choices.experiment: Underline each action you can support. Replace unsupported actions with what you actually observed. Then make one revision for rhythm without adding a fact.
choices.compare: Did the energetic version gain its energy by pretending to know?
choices.exception: A fictional narrator may make an unsupported claim deliberately. Give the reader a reason to notice that.

choices.label: Choose the exact meaning before choosing a rhythm.
choices.reason: The sentence’s sharpest word may also be its least exact. Decide whether you mean unanswered, misplaced, ignored, or forgotten before arranging the rhythm.
choices.counter: Accuracy need not leave the sentence inert. Once the facts are secure, a well-chosen action can do more than a general description.
choices.experiment: Write the known fact in the fewest useful words. Add one observed action. Read both aloud, choosing the version that suits the paragraph’s purpose.
choices.compare: What did the extra action teach the reader?
choices.exception: Do not trim a necessary qualification just to make a cleaner sentence.

moments.title: The minor character has the best lines.
moments.setup: The sister was meant to interrupt dinner. Now she is more interesting than the host, and the scene keeps following her.
moments.example: “I have eleven minutes,” she said, taking the chair nearest the door.

choices.label: Follow her purpose for a page.
choices.reason: The interruption may contain a private urgency the original plan ignored. Give it enough room to become an action.
choices.counter: A vivid character can take over a scene. Giving her a purpose does not automatically give her the whole story.
choices.experiment: Write the scene from the sister’s position, then from the host’s. Give each one detail the other fails to notice. Return to the original viewpoint and keep one change.
choices.compare: Does the sister become more specific without making everyone else a prop?
choices.exception: If the host is the only narrator, keep that viewpoint; it can still show what the sister needs.

choices.label: Keep her purpose, but reduce her share of the scene.
choices.reason: The scene may gain pressure if her private urgency remains visible in a small number of actions.
choices.counter: Compression can turn her back into a category. Make sure the cut preserves the detail that resists the host’s easy verdict.
choices.experiment: Reduce her speech by half. Keep one action that contradicts the host’s judgment of her. Read the scene without the label “selfish.”
choices.compare: Does the action carry a conflict that the label merely announced?
choices.exception: If the smaller part cannot hold what matters, consider whether the story has found a new center.
